title.narrative: UNESCO Our Rights, Our Lives, Our Future Phase II (2023 - 2027)
UNESCO Our Rights, Our Lives, Our Future Phase II (2023 - 2027)

description.narrative:
1) Support an enabling policy and institutional environment for implementation of school health programmes that include CSE and prevention of school violence.
2) Support countries to scale up and strengthen the delivery of accurate, rights-based, gender transformative and good quality teaching and learning on CSE and school violence prevention.
3) Empower AYP and respect their right to make decisions and drive changes in their lives and communities using digital innovations.
4) Promote the creation of safer, inclusive school and community environments with linkages to accessible, youth-friendly SRH services.
5) Strengthen programme implementation through evidence generated from monitoring, evaluation, research and learning.

Det övergripande målet är att förbättra SRHR, jämställdhet och utbildning för unga i Afrika söder om Sahara genom att minska antalet nya fall av hiv och andra sexuellt överförbara infektioner, förebygga tidiga och oönskade graviditeter liksom skolvåld, och därigenom säkerställa ungas välbefinnande. Detta ska uppnås genom följande delmål: 1. Stödja en möjliggörande policy och institutionell miljö för genomförande av elevhälsoprogram som inkluderar sexualundervisning och förebyggande av skolvåld. 2. Stödja länder att skala upp och stärka tillhandahållandet av korrekt, rättighetsbaserad, gender transformativ och högkvalitativ undervisning och lärande om sexualundervisning och förebyggande av våld i skolan. 3. Stärka unga och respektera deras rätt att fatta beslut och driva förändringar i sina liv och samhällen med hjälp av digitala innovationer. 4. Främja säkrare och inkluderande skol- och samhällsmiljöer med tillgång till ungdomsvänliga SRH-tjänster. 5. Stärka programmets genomförande genom att generera evidens från uppföljning, utvärdering, forskning och lärande.

The programme aims to improve SRHR, gender equality and education for adolescents and young people in sub-Saharan Africa by preventing HIV and other sexually transmitted infections, early and unintended pregnancies, and school violence, and thereby ensuring young people's well-being. This will be achieved through five objectives: 1) Support an enabling policy and institutional environment for implementation of school health programmes that include comprehensive sexuality education and prevention of school violence. 2) Support countries to scale up and strengthen the delivery of accurate, rights-based, gender transformative and good quality teaching and learning on comprehensive sexuality education and school violence prevention. 3) Empower adolescents and young people and respect their right to make decisions and drive changes in their lives and communities using digital innovations. 4) Promote the creation of safer, inclusive school and community environments with linkages to accessible, youth-friendly SRH services. 5) Strengthen programme implementation through evidence generated from monitoring, evaluation, research and learning.

The second phase of the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organizations (UNESCOs) Our Rights, Our Lives, Our, Our Future (O3) programme commenced in July 2023. The initial six months, from July to December, focused on establishing strategic priorities and partnerships for the programmes advancement in the new phase. During the last year, in 2024, the programme focused on consolidating the results achieved in Phase I and working the new objectives in Phase II on empowering young people to learn and thrive in safe, inclusive, and supportive environments. The programme O3 has shown impressive results during Phase I and it continues to reach ambitious targets during Phase II of the programme. The programme has reached over 34 million learners since 2018, equipping them with reliable, scientifically accurate information on comprehensive sexuality education (CSE).
Objective 1: In 2024, the O3 programme achieved significant milestones in strengthening the institutional and policy environment for comprehensive sexuality education (CSE) across sub-Saharan Africa. At the regional level, the programme reinforced coordination and steering mechanisms supporting the implementation of the Eastern and Southern Africa (ESA) and West and Central Africa (WCA) Ministerial Commitments. The programme also achieved a historic engagement with religious leaders across the Southern African Development Community (SADC) region. In a landmark dialogue facilitated jointly with UNFPA, Save the Children, and IOM, faith leaders acknowledged the alignment between CSE and values of protection, guidance, and empowerment, culminating in a ground breaking declaration where they committed to championing CSE and AYPs sexual and reproductive health and rights. By the end of 2024, nine countries had implemented national strategies aimed at building support for CSE and proactively addressing resistance. In parallel, by the end of 2024, a cumulative total of 23 countries had integrated intersectoral policies linking education, health, and violence response services. Through sustained advocacy, over 1,100 policymakers were engaged to influence and shape responsive policies grounded in national realities and specific adolescents and youth people needs. Despite these strides, persistent challenges remain. Sociopolitical resistance to CSE, often driven by misinformation, continues to hinder progress in some contexts. In addition, limited domestic financing constrains the scale and sustainability of CSE delivery.
Objective 2: Objective 2: The O3 programme advanced efforts to improve the delivery of quality rights based gender transformative CSE by different means. Several countries such as Eswatini, Lesotho, Tanzania, and Zambia have begun utilizing additional resources from the Building Strong Foundations (BSF) initiative to guide curriculum reviews and teacher training. The College Hub model was initiated in Eswatini, Lesotho, and Malawi (joining Zambia), marking a strategic shift toward a more sustainable and institutionalized approach to strengthening teacher capacities in CSE delivery. Across the ESA and WCA regions, the programme strengthened the capacity of over 50,000 preservice and 41,000 in-service teachers, contributing to delivery of CSE and school related violence prevention education for more than 23.4 million learners in nearly 190,000 schools. However, the foundational time required to initiate and establish the College Hub model contributed to slower implementation of training activities across the four countries, resulting in missed teacher training targets overall. Full-scale implementation is anticipated in 2025, as the model becomes fully established and operational in these countries. In Zambia, UNESCO worked actively with Minister of Education to develop the curriculum for the standardized training manuals for Life Skills Health Education (LSHE), that replaced CSE. Despite the LSHE learning material being finalized, materials for each grade level are yet to be developed/printed and distributed.
Objective 3: The use of digital innovations continued to expand in 2024, reaching over 30.5 million young people through various platforms and tools. Nearly 900,000 young people participated in online safety campaigns in 2024 alone, enhancing their ability to navigate digital risks. While notable progress was made in expanding the reach of digital innovations, UNESCO has noted some challenges such as user retention and limited connectivity in politically unstable contexts impacted sustained engagement. Addressing these challenges remains a priority, with ongoing efforts to enhance content relevance, improve user experience, and ensure broader, more equitable access to digital platforms.
Objective 4: In 2024, UNESCO has very involved in the 2nd Southern Africa Symposium on Preventing Gender Based Violence reinforced regional commitment to advancing gender equality and safe learning environments. They also worked towards the scale up of the Connect with Respect programme a curriculum based tool for addressing school related gender based violence (SRGBV) to eleven countries across the ESA region. New additions included Kenya, Namibia, Uganda, and South Africa, joining Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho, Malawi, Tanzania, Zambia, and Zimbabwe. In 2024 alone, over 1.1 million community members and opinion leaders were reached through face-to-face engagement, through strategic partnerships aimed at addressing GBV, early and unintended pregnancy (EUP), and child marriage in a more holistic manner. Parent teacher associations (PTAs) played a pivotal role in reinforcing school community linkages, with over 46,000 PTA members sensitized on CSE, GBV, EUP, and child marriage, further embedding community-level support structures in the work. In parallel, the O3 programme supported national policy advancements: Lesotho revised its school violence policies to enhance protection mechanisms for learners in Congo, the National Strategy for Juvenile Delinquency Prevention reinforced a national youth protection framework and in Senegal, two harmonized training modules were developed to address SRGBV across both elementary and secondary education, ensuring a standardized, cross sectoral approach. As part of their advocacy work with Parliamentarians, UNESCO Zambia is playing an active role in the task force working on changing the age of consent for adolescents to access SRHR services. Consultations are ongoing between the Task Force and the Attorney General, Ministry of Health and Ministry of Community Development to draft statutory instruments and engage in a law review of the Children's Code Act.
Objective 5: In collaboration with the World Health Organization, UNESCO continued to support countries in implementing the largescale Global School Health Survey (GSHS) and Global School Health Policies and Practices Survey (GSHPPS). These surveys are critical in addressing data gaps, establishing essential baselines, and providing valuable insights into adolescent wellbeing and education outcomes. By the end of the year, six countries (Botswana, Gabon, Lesotho, Namibia, Tanzania Zanzibar, and Zimbabwe) had successfully completed the GSHS, with Ghana completing the GSHPPS. Overall, 24 research pieces and related knowledge products which were produced. The CSE opposition research in Ethiopia, Kenya, and Malawi systematically mapped the composition, influence, and extent of infiltration of anti-CSE actors and their narratives. Across the five objectives, UNESCO has surpassed a majority of the targets for 2024, including the number of primary and secondary schools that provided life skills based HIV and sexuality education in the previous academic year (189 804 schools were reached).
